title: Pick parts off a slow and a fast lane in the order they will leave reach, not the order they arrive
instruction: Four parts will come out on the two lanes, two on each. Put every part in the grey bin before it rides under the cover on the left. The near lane runs five times as fast as the far lane.
context: Where lanes run side by side at different speeds, the part to take next is the one that will leave reach first, not the one that came out first or is nearest the end: a part on a fast lane can come out later, further back, and still run out sooner. Done by: line operators, packers, and pick-and-place robots on sorting lines.
setup: The two arm bases stand 61 cm apart on an oak table (1.10 x 1.30 m) whose side edges are 65 cm either side of the midpoint between the bases. Two straight conveyor lanes run parallel to the line through the bases, their centre lines 29 cm (near lane) and 41 cm (far lane) in front of it. Each lane has two dark steel rails (1.5 x 1.5 cm, 72.5 cm long) 2 cm either side of its centre line, from 9 cm right to 63.5 cm left of the midpoint. Grey sheet-steel covers hide both lanes except one window open from the table up, from 13 to 47 cm left of the midpoint. Each cover is a tunnel over both lanes: two side walls (1 cm thick, 9.2 cm tall) standing on the table, their inner faces 24.25 and 45.75 cm in front of the bases, a flat roof (23.5 cm wide, 0.8 cm thick) on them, and an end wall closing its outer end. The feed cover runs from 13 cm left of the midpoint to its end wall, whose inner face is 9 cm right of it; the run-out cover runs from 47 cm left of the midpoint (the end line) to its end wall, whose inner face is 63.5 cm left of it. Each part is a bare aluminium cube (4 x 4 x 4 cm, 170 g) standing in the middle of its own grey steel carrier (6.5 x 6.5 x 1.5 cm), which rides 2 mm above its lane's rails, square to them. At the start each lane has two carriers under the feed cover, centred 8 cm left (lead) and 1 cm right (second) of the midpoint. A grey plastic open bin (14 x 14 cm outside, 12 x 12 cm inside, 1 cm floor, 6 cm walls) stands on the table square to the lanes, its centre 14 cm in front of the bases and 0.5 cm toward the midpoint from the left arm's base. Both lanes carry parts from the robot's right to its left: the near lane at 10 cm/s, the far lane at 2 cm/s. Each carrier stands still until its release time, then speeds up over 0.5 s, cruises at its lane's speed, and slows over 0.5 s to a stop under the run-out cover (the lead carriers 59.5 cm, the second ones 50.5 cm left of the midpoint). Release times from the start of the trial: far lane lead 0 s, near lane lead 3.3 s, far lane second 6.25 s, near lane second 13.15 s. So the cubes come out of the feed cover (front face at its mouth) and reach the end line (centre at the run-out cover's mouth) at: far 1: 1.75 s and 19.75 s; near 1: 3.85 s and 7.45 s; far 2: 12.5 s and 30.5 s; near 2: 14.6 s and 18.2 s. The arms start in their ready pose with open grippers; only the left arm reaches the window and the bin.
scoring: 0.25 for each cube lying in the bin when the trial ends: its centre inside the bin's walls, its underside below the rim (on the floor or on another cube), still. 1.0 once all four lie there for 1 s, which ends the trial. A cube must go straight from its carrier into the bin: one that spends 0.5 s or more in a row neither on its own carrier, nor held in a gripper (its centre within 5 cm of the point between the finger pads), nor over the inside of the bin is lost and scores 0 even if it later reaches the bin (put down on the table, a cover or another carrier, or knocked off the lane). A cube that rides under the run-out cover is out of reach and scores 0. So 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 or 1.0.
reset_notes: Put the four carriers back under the feed cover at their start positions, a cube centred on each, and start the release timer with the trial.
fidelity: The carriers follow their paths exactly, like servo-driven lane carriers: the arms can't push or stop them (a real drive would fault if blocked). They ride 2 mm above the rails; a lifted cube's carrier slides on from under it. The cubes have the station's rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), more than aluminium on steel, far above what their 0.31 m/s² peak needs. A real line would use belts and a timed escapement; here each cube rides its own carrier released at a fixed time.
